transcript.text: micrwave keeps tripping the eletric, not every time but like 1 in 3 when i press start, whole kitchen goes off. had to reset the fuse box 4 times today

This is a serious electrical safety issue. The fact that you have had to reset your consumer unit (fuse box) four times in one day indicates a significant fault that could lead to fire or electric shock if not addressed properly.

### 🚨 Immediate Safety Advice
1.  Stop using the microwave immediately. Do not plug it back in until it has been inspected by a qualified electrician.
2.  Do not keep resetting the breaker as a "fix." The breaker is tripping to protect your wiring from overheating and catching fire. Ignoring this risk is dangerous.
3.  If you smell burning, see smoke, or hear buzzing/arcing sounds near the socket or microwave, evacuate the area and call emergency services.

---

### Why Is This Happening?
The pattern ("1 in 3 times") suggests an intermittent fault, which is often harder to diagnose but can be just as dangerous. Here are the most likely causes:

#### 1. Internal Fault in the Microwave
• A failing magnetron, capacitor, or internal wiring short may only trigger when certain components heat up or draw peak current at specific moments during the cooking cycle.
• Moisture buildup inside the microwave (from splatters) can cause intermittent arcing to earth, tripping a RCD/GFCI (Residual Current Device).

#### 2. Loose Wiring in the Socket or Circuit
• A loose neutral or live connection at the wall socket or in the junction box behind it can create resistance and heat. When the microwave draws high current (especially during startup), the poor connection causes a voltage drop or arc, tripping the breaker.
• This is common in older kitchens where sockets have been moved or installed poorly.

#### 3. Overloaded Circuit
• Microwaves draw significant power (often 10–15 amps). If this microwave shares a circuit with other high-draw appliances (toaster, kettle, oven), starting the microwave might push the total load over the breaker’s limit.
• However, if only the microwave is on and it still trips, overload is less likely than a fault.

#### 4. Faulty Breaker or RCD
• The circuit breaker itself may be worn out or sensitive. If it has tripped many times already (you mentioned 4 resets today), it could be degraded and now tripping on minor fluctuations that it wouldn’t have before.

---

### What You Should Do Next

#### ✅ Step 1: Isolate the Problem
• Unplug the microwave from the wall.
• Try turning on other high-draw appliances in the kitchen (kettle, toaster) one at a time. If they work fine and don’t trip the breaker, the issue is likely isolated to the microwave or its specific socket.

#### ✅ Step 2: Check for Other Symptoms
• Does the microwave spark inside when running?
• Does it make unusual noises?
• Is the plug/socket warm to the touch?
• If yes to any of these, do not use it again.

#### ✅ Step 3: Call a Qualified Electrician
• This is not a DIY fix. You need a licensed electrician to:
• Test the microwave’s insulation resistance and earth continuity.
• Check the socket wiring for tightness and signs of arcing/burning.
• Verify if the circuit is overloaded or if the breaker needs replacement.
• Mention that it trips intermittently (1 in 3 times) and has required multiple resets. This helps them prioritize RCD/earth leakage tests.

#### ✅ Step 4: Temporary Workaround (If You Must Use It)
• Do not use this microwave until inspected. If you have another kitchen outlet on a different circuit, you might try it there temporarily to see if the problem follows the appliance or stays with the socket/circuit. Only do this if you are confident in your safety knowledge and the new outlet is properly grounded. Even then, stop immediately if it trips again.

---

### Summary
• Likely Cause: Faulty microwave internal component OR loose wiring at the socket.
• Risk: Fire or electric shock due to overheating/arc faults.
• Action: Unplug and do not use. Hire a qualified electrician to inspect the appliance, socket, and circuit breaker.

Please prioritize safety—electrical fires are often caused by ignored intermittent tripping.
